entries.daa005e2242326fb3944ab78db935f447383c553: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14108"/><div sID="gen27246" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14108"/><hi type="bold">25. For when they shall rise from the dead, they neither marry, nor are given in marriage--</hi>"neither can they die any more" (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.36">Lu 20:36</reference>). Marriage is ordained to perpetuate the human family; but as there will be no breaches by death in the future state, this ordinance will cease.<div eID="gen27246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but are as the angels which are in heaven--</hi>In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.36">Lu 20:36</reference>) it is "equal unto the angels." But as the subject is death and resurrection, we are not warranted to extend the equality here taught beyond the one point--the immortality of their nature. A beautiful clause is added in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.36">Lu 20:36</reference>)--"and are the children of God"--not in respect of character, which is not here spoken of, but of nature--"being the children of the resurrection," as rising to an undecaying existence (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.21">Ro 8:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.23">23</reference>), and so being the children of their Father's immortality (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:16</reference>). <div eID="gen27247" type="x-p"/>
entries.425f6c6b6ac84544b878fc7c2998486120decd19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14109"/><div sID="gen27248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14109"/><hi type="bold">26. And as touching the dead, that they rise: have ye not read in the book of Moses--</hi>"even Moses" (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.37">Lu 20:37</reference>), whom they had just quoted for the purpose of entangling Him.<div eID="gen27248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how in the bush God spake unto him--</hi>either "at the bush," as the same expression is rendered in <reference osisRef="Luke.20.37">Lu 20:37</reference>, that is, when he was there; or "in the [section of his history regarding the] bush." The structure of our verse suggests the latter sense, which is not unusual.<div eID="gen27249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.3.6">Ex 3:6</reference>). <div eID="gen27250" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6c3b5e2781d76b31f925819f9cc3c73cbc82036: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14110"/><div sID="gen27251" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14110"/><hi type="bold">27. He is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living--</hi>not "the God of dead but [the God] of living persons." The word in brackets is almost certainly an addition to the genuine text, and critical editors exclude it. "For all live unto Him" (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.38">Lu 20:38</reference>)--"in His view," or "in His estimation." This last statement--found only in Luke--though adding nothing to the argument, is an important additional illustration. It is true, indeed, that to God no human being is dead or ever will be, but all mankind sustain an abiding conscious relation to Him; but the "all" here means "those who shall be accounted worthy to obtain that world." These sustain a gracious covenant relation to God which cannot be dissolved. (Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.6.10">Ro 6:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.11">11</reference>). In this sense our Lord affirms that for Moses to call the Lord the "God" of His patriarchal servants, if at that moment they had no existence, would be unworthy of Him. He "would be ashamed to be called their God, if He had not prepared for them a city" (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.16">He 11:16</reference>). It was concluded by some of the early Fathers, from our Lord's resting His proof of the Resurrection on such a passage as this, instead of quoting some much clearer testimonies of the Old Testament, that the Sadducees, to whom this was addressed, acknowledged the authority of no part of the Old Testament but the Pentateuch; and this opinion has held its ground even till now. But as there is no ground for it in the New Testament, so Josephus is silent upon it; merely saying that they rejected the Pharisaic traditions. It was because the Pentateuch was regarded by all classes as the fundamental source of the Hebrew religion, and all the succeeding books of the Old Testament but as developments of it, that our Lord would show that even there the doctrine of the Resurrection was taught. And all the rather does He select this passage, as being not a bare annunciation of the doctrine in question, but as expressive of that glorious truth out of which the Resurrection springs. "And when the multitude heard this" (says <reference osisRef="Matt.22.23">Mt 22:23</reference>), "they were astonished at His doctrine." "Then," adds <reference osisRef="Luke.20.39">Lu 20:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.20.40">40</reference>, "certain of the scribes answering said, Master, thou hast well said"--enjoying His victory over the Sadducees. "And after that they durst not ask Him any [question at all]"--neither party could; both being for the time utterly foiled.<div eID="gen27251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27252" type="x-p"/> The Great Commandment (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.28-Mark.12.34">Mr 12:28-34</reference>).<div eID="gen27252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27253" type="x-p"/> "But when the Pharisees had heard that He had put the Sadducees to silence, they were gathered together" (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.34">Mt 22:34</reference>). <div eID="gen27253" type="x-p"/>
entries.e64fa3b0105733655e589c694181e4261928c176: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14111"/><div sID="gen27254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14111"/><hi type="bold">28. And one of the scribes--</hi>"a lawyer," says Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.35">Mt 22:35</reference>); that is, teacher of the law.<div eID="gen27254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came, and having heard them reasoning together, and perceiving that he had answered them well, asked him--</hi>manifestly in no bad spirit. When Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.35">Mt 22:35</reference>) therefore says he came "tempting," or "trying him," as one of the Pharisaic party who seemed to enjoy the defeat He had given to the Sadducees, we may suppose that though somewhat priding himself upon his insight into the law, and not indisposed to measure his knowledge with One in whom he had not yet learned to believe, he was nevertheless an honest-hearted, fair disputant.<div eID="gen27255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Which is the first commandment of all?--</hi>first in importance; the primary, leading commandment, the most fundamental one. This was a question which, with some others, divided the Jewish teachers into rival schools. Our Lord's answer is in a strain of respect very different from what He showed to cavillers--ever observing His own direction, "Give not that which is holy to the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine; lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you" (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Mt 7:6</reference>). <div eID="gen27256" type="x-p"/>
entries.2912e60fdb6a1258e7fe50140eac05a6a5a19f2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14112"/><div sID="gen27257" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14112"/><hi type="bold">29. And Jesus answered him, The first of all the commandments is--</hi>The readings here vary considerably. Tischendorf and Tregelles read simply, "the first is"; and they are followed by Meyer and Alford. But though the authority for the precise form of the received text is slender, a form almost identical with it seems to have most weight of authority. Our Lord here gives His explicit sanction to the distinction between commandments of a more fundamental and primary character, and commandments of a more dependent and subordinate nature; a distinction of which it is confidently asserted by a certain class of critics that the Jews knew nothing, that our Lord and His apostles nowhere lay down, and which has been invented by Christian divines. (Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.23.23">Mt 23:23</reference>).<div eID="gen27257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hear, O Israel; the Lord our God is one Lord--</hi>This every devout Jew recited twice every day, and the Jews do it to this day; thus keeping up the great ancient national protest against the polytheisms and pantheisms of the heathen world: it is the great utterance of the national faith in One Living and Personal God--"One Jehovah!" <div eID="gen27258" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e7979b3679a3e446bed2dab478e3a35743b385d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14113"/><div sID="gen27259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14113"/><hi type="bold">30. And thou shalt--</hi>We have here the language of law, expressive of God's claims. What then are we here bound down to do? One word is made to express it. And what a word! Had the essence of the divine law consisted in deeds, it could not possibly have been expressed in a single word; for no one deed is comprehensive of all others embraced in the law. But as it consists in an affection of the soul, one word suffices to express it--but only one. Fear, though due to God and enjoined by Him, is limited in its sphere and distant in character. Trust, hope, and the like, though essential features of a right state of heart towards God, are called into action only by personal necessity, and so are--in a good sense, it is true, but still are properly--selfish affections; that is to say, they have respect to our own well-being. But LOVE is an all-inclusive affection, embracing not only every other affection proper to its object, but all that is proper to be done to its object; for as love spontaneously seeks to please its object, so, in the case of men to God, it is the native well spring of a voluntary obedience. It is, besides, the most personal of all affections. One may fear an event, one may hope for an event, one may rejoice in an event; but one can love only a Person. It is the tenderest, the most unselfish, the most divine of all affections. Such, then, is the affection in which the essence of the divine law is declared to consist.<div eID="gen27259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou shalt love--</hi>We now come to the glorious Object of that demanded affection.<div eID="gen27260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou shalt love the Lord, thy God--</hi>that is, Jehovah, the Self-Existent One, who has revealed Himself as the "I Am," and there is none else; who, though by His name Jehovah apparently at an unapproachable distance from His finite creatures, yet bears to Thee a real and definite relationship, out of which arises His claim and Thy duty--of LOVE. But with what are we to love Him? Four things are here specified. First, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God"<div eID="gen27261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with thy heart--</hi>This sometimes means "the whole inner man" (as <reference osisRef="Prov.4.23">Pr 4:23</reference>); but that cannot be meant here; for then the other three particulars would be superfluous. Very often it means "our emotional nature"--the seat of feeling as distinguished from our intellectual nature or the seat of thought, commonly called the "mind" (as in <reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">Php 4:7</reference>). But neither can this be the sense of it here; for here the heart is distinguished both from the "mind" and the "soul." The "heart," then, must here mean the sincerity of both the thoughts and the feelings; in other words, uprightness or true-heartedness, as opposed to a hypocritical or divided affection. But next, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God" with thy soul. This is designed to command our emotional nature: Thou shalt put feeling or warmth into thine affection. Further, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God"<div eID="gen27262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with thy mind--</hi>This commands our intellectual nature: Thou shalt put intelligence into thine affection--in opposition to a blind devotion, or mere devoteeism. Lastly, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God"<div eID="gen27263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with thy strength--</hi>This commands our energies: Thou shalt put intensity into thine affection--"Do it with thy might" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">Ec 9:10</reference>). Taking these four things together, the command of the Law is, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy powers--with a sincere, a fervid, an intelligent, an energetic love." But this is not all that the Law demands. God will have all these qualities in their most perfect exercise. "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God," says the Law, "with all thy heart," or, with perfect sincerity; "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy soul," or, with the utmost fervor; "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy mind," or, in the fullest exercise of an enlightened reason; and "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy strength," or, with the whole energy of our being! So much for the First Commandment. <div eID="gen27264" type="x-p"/>
entries.77818b3ed5f3cb794034e97c731b66786aea59eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14114"/><div sID="gen27265" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14114"/><hi type="bold">31. And the second is like--</hi>"unto it" (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.39">Mt 22:39</reference>); as demanding the same affection, and only the extension of it, in its proper measure, to the creatures of Him whom we thus love--our brethren in the participation of the same nature, and neighbors, as connected with us by ties that render each dependent upon and necessary to the other.<div eID="gen27265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27266" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou shall love thy neighbour as thyself--</hi>Now, as we are not to love ourselves supremely, this is virtually a command, in the first place, not to love our neighbor with all our heart and soul and mind and strength. And thus it is a condemnation of the idolatry of the creature. Our supreme and uttermost affection is to be reserved for God. But as sincerely as ourselves we are to love all mankind, and with the same readiness to do and suffer for them as we should reasonably desire them to show to us. The golden rule (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.12">Mt 7:12</reference>) is here our best interpreter of the nature and extent of these claims.<div eID="gen27266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">There is none other commandment greater than these--</hi>or, as in <reference osisRef="Matt.22.40">Mt 22:40</reference>, "On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets" (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.5.17">Mt 5:17</reference>). It is as if He had said, "This is all Scripture in a nutshell; the whole law of human duty in a portable, pocket form." Indeed, it is so simple that a child may understand it, so brief that all may remember it, so comprehensive as to embrace all possible cases. And from its very nature it is unchangeable. It is inconceivable that God should require from his rational creatures anything less, or in substance anything else, under any dispensation, in any world, at any period throughout eternal duration. He cannot but claim this--all this--alike in heaven, in earth, and in hell! And this incomparable summary of the divine law belonged to the Jewish religion! As it shines in its own self-evidencing splendor, so it reveals its own true source. The religion from which the world has received it could be none other than a God-given religion! <div eID="gen27267" type="x-p"/>
entries.2dd9036ecfa7e8e65584b962994a438742b93478: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14115"/><div sID="gen27268" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14115"/><hi type="bold">32. And the scribe said unto him, Well, Master--</hi>Teacher.<div eID="gen27268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou hast said the truth: for there is one God; and there is none other but he--</hi>The genuine text here seems clearly to have been, "There is one," without the word "God"; and so nearly all critical editors and expositors read. <div eID="gen27269" type="x-p"/>
entries.df8f85263be664b0ec44f5bfbf5f87f916a558a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14116"/><div sID="gen27270" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14116"/><hi type="bold">33. And to love him with all the heart ... and to love his neighbour as himself, is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices--</hi>more, that is, than all positive institutions; thereby showing insight into the essential difference between what is moral and in its own nature unchangeable, and what is obligatory only because enjoined, and only so long as enjoined. <div eID="gen27270" type="x-p"/>
entries.54260668404f5db5e814514bfccf8bf3b27ee635: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14117"/><div sID="gen27271" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14117"/><hi type="bold">34. And when Jesus saw that he answered discreetly--</hi>rather, "intelligently," or "sensibly"; not only in a good spirit, but with a promising measure of insight into spiritual things.<div eID="gen27271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he said unto him, Thou art not far from the kingdom of God--</hi>for he had but to follow out a little further what he seemed sincerely to own, to find his way into the kingdom. He needed only the experience of another eminent scribe who at a later period said, "We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin": who exclaimed, "O wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me?" but who added, "I thank God through Jesus Christ!" (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.14">Ro 7:14</reference>, 24, 25). Perhaps among the "great company of the priests" and other Jewish ecclesiastics who "were obedient to the faith," almost immediately after the day of Pentecost (<reference osisRef="Acts.6.7">Ac 6:7</reference>), this upright lawyer was one. But for all his nearness to the Kingdom of God, it may be he never entered it.<div eID="gen27272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27273" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And no man after that durst ask any question--</hi>all feeling that they were no match for Him, and that it was vain to enter the lists with Him.<div eID="gen27273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27274" type="x-p"/> Christ Baffles the Pharisees Regarding David (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.35-Mark.12.37">Mr 12:35-37</reference>). <div eID="gen27274" type="x-p"/>
entries.cae5a3444dde1d46005a40dc2c33d24523886caf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14118"/><div sID="gen27275" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14118"/><hi type="bold">35. And Jesus answered and said, while he taught in the temple--</hi>and "while the Pharisees were gathered together" (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.41">Mt 22:41</reference>).<div eID="gen27275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">How say the scribes that Christ is the son of David?--</hi>How come they to give it out that Messiah is to be the son of David? In Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.42">Mt 22:42</reference>), Jesus asks them, "What think ye of Christ?" or of the promised and expected Messiah? "Whose son is He [to be]? They say unto Him, The son of David." The sense is the same. "He saith unto them, How then doth David in spirit call Him Lord?" (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.42">Mt 22:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.43">43</reference>). <div eID="gen27276" type="x-p"/>
entries.a864b1cb40ff9fe09c6ffffb0d60f52ec5075c29: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14119"/><div sID="gen27277" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14119"/><hi type="bold">36. For David himself said by the Holy Ghost, The Lord said to my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Psa 110:1</reference>). <div eID="gen27277" type="x-p"/>
entries.65b5db14912c472b975f2ec5af635dd440a4b473: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14120"/><div sID="gen27278" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14120"/><hi type="bold">37. David therefore himself calleth him Lord; and whence is he then his son?--</hi>There is but one solution of this difficulty. Messiah is at once inferior to David as his son according to the flesh, and superior to him as the Lord of a kingdom of which David is himself a subject, not the sovereign. The human and divine natures of Christ, and the spirituality of His kingdom--of which the highest earthly sovereigns are honored if they be counted worthy to be its subjects--furnish the only key to this puzzle.<div eID="gen27278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27279" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And the common people--</hi>the immense crowd.<div eID="gen27279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard him gladly--</hi>"And no man was able to answer Him a word; neither durst any man from that day forth ask Him any more questions" (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.46">Mt 22:46</reference>).<div eID="gen27280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27281" type="x-p"/> The Scribes Denounced (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.38-Mark.12.40">Mr 12:38-40</reference>). <div eID="gen27281" type="x-p"/>
entries.5dfb5aa98da1ff10bddd13a08502f850db344686: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14121"/><div sID="gen27282" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14121"/><hi type="bold">38. And he said unto them in his doctrine--</hi>rather, "in His teaching"; implying that this was but a specimen of an extended discourse, which Matthew gives in full (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.1-Matt.23.39">Mt 23:1-39</reference>). Luke says (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.45">Lu 20:45</reference>) this was "in the audience of all the people said unto His disciples."<div eID="gen27282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beware of the scribes, which love--</hi>or like.<div eID="gen27283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27284" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to go in long clothing--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Matt.23.5">Mt 23:5</reference>).<div eID="gen27284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27285" type="x-p"/> and love salutations in the market-places, <div eID="gen27285" type="x-p"/>
entries.97695daf33bca1c15e4ebf4d8a180cb89f3ded84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14122"/><div sID="gen27286" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14122"/><hi type="bold">39. And the chief seats in the synagogues, and the uppermost rooms--</hi>or positions.<div eID="gen27286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at feasts--</hi>On this love of distinction, see on <reference osisRef="Luke.14.7">Lu 14:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.5">Mt 6:5</reference>. <div eID="gen27287" type="x-p"/>
entries.440e1f916c1d37383107aef30c86056d71daf169: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14123"/><div sID="gen27288" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14123"/>40. Which devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayers: <hi type="bold">these shall receive greater damnation--</hi>They took advantage of their helpless condition and confiding character to obtain possession of their property, while by their "long prayers" they made them believe they were raised far above "filthy lucre." So much the "greater damnation" awaited them. (Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.23.33">Mt 23:33</reference>). A lifelike description this of the Romish clergy, the true successors of "the scribes." <div eID="gen27288" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14124"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.12.41-Mark.12.44">Mr 12:41-44</reference>. The Widow's Two Mites. ( = <reference osisRef="Luke.21.1-Luke.21.4">Lu 21:1-4</reference>).</title> <title type="x-s3">See on <reference osisRef="Luke.21.1-Luke.21.4">Lu 21:1-4</reference>.</title> <div sID="gen27289" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Mark.12"/>

entries.f0fb82bf320df90b6df928d2d30d1160b8834a50: <div eID="gen39571" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen39572" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39573" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39573" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39572" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39574" type="x-p"/> The parable of the vineyard let out to wicked husbandmen, <reference osisRef="Mar.12.1-Mar.12.12">Mar 12:1-12</reference>. The Pharisees and Herodians question him about paying tribute to Caesar, <reference osisRef="Mar.12.13-Mar.12.17">Mar 12:13-17</reference>. The Sadducees question him about the resurrection, <reference osisRef="Mar.12.18-Mar.12.27">Mar 12:18-27</reference>. A scribe questions him concerning the chief commandment of the law, <reference osisRef="Mar.12.28-Mar.12.34">Mar 12:28-34</reference>. Christ asks the scribes why the Messiah is called David's son, <reference osisRef="Mar.12.35-Mar.12.37">Mar 12:35-37</reference>. He warns his disciples against the scribes, <reference osisRef="Mar.12.38-Mar.12.40">Mar 12:38-40</reference>. Of the widow that cast two mites into the treasury, <reference osisRef="Mar.12.41-Mar.12.44">Mar 12:41-44</reference>. <div eID="gen39574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39575" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39576" type="x-p"/> A certain man planted a vineyard - See this parable explained, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.33-Mat.21.41">Mat 21:33-41</reference> (note).
entries.7c4bf58c00df30a1a22eb18374c6aad0f3950301: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen39576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39577" type="x-p"/> At him they cast stones and wounded him in the head - Or rather, as most learned men agree, they made short work of it, εκεφαλαιωσαν. We have followed the Vulgate, illum in capite vulneraverunt, in translating the original, wounded him in the head, in which signification, I believe, the word is found in no Greek writer. Ανακεφαλαιοομαι signifies to sum up, to comprise, and is used in this sense by St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.9">Rom 13:9</reference>. From the parable we learn that these people were determined to hear no reason, to do no justice, and to keep the possession and the produce by violence; therefore they fulfilled their purpose in the fullest and speediest manner, which seems to be what the evangelist intended to express by the word in question. Mr. Wakefield translates, They speedily sent him away; others think the meaning is, They shaved their heads and made them look ridiculously; this is much to the same purpose, but I prefer, They made short work of it. Dr. Lightfoot, De Dieu, and others, agree in the sense given above; and this will appear the more probable, if the word λιθοβολησαντες, they cast stones, be omitted, as it is by BDL, the Coptic, Vulgate, and all the Itala.
entries.2073f412afd9c6e24eff541ae0b1a9a48f741592: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen39577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39578" type="x-p"/> This is the heir - So they appear to have acknowledged in their consciences that this was the Messiah, the heir of all things. <div eID="gen39578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39579" type="x-p"/> The inheritance shall be ours - By slaying him we shall maintain our authority, and keep possession of our revenues.
entries.e09fa99f3453767c4de36f004139bdd37f2c2fcd: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen39579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39580" type="x-p"/> And will give the vineyard unto others - The vineyard must not perish with the husbandmen; it is still capable of producing much fruit, if it be properly cultivated. I will give it into the care of new vine-dressers, the evangelists and apostles. - And under their ministry, multitudes were brought to God before the destruction of Jerusalem.
entries.a1b86a797251a72458499e94f5c24b3e2b190d46: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen39580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39581" type="x-p"/> And they send unto him - See this, and to <reference osisRef="Mar.12.17">Mar 12:17</reference>, largely explained on <reference osisRef="Mat.22.15-Mat.22.22">Mat 22:15-22</reference> (note).
entries.76a67d8bb7502467ad6a612ac5d07dabef9f49a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen39581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39582" type="x-p"/> Shall we give, or shall we not give? - This is wanting in the Codex Bezae, and in several versions.
entries.c2ea5fe9f2aa141f36d629c9b8d0c46beb0eadb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen39582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39583" type="x-p"/> See this question, concerning the resurrection, explained in detail on <reference osisRef="Mat.22.23-Mat.22.32">Mat 22:23-32</reference> (note).
entries.acc5699671a3a27807d2096f66cd42e17e09a4a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen39583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39584" type="x-p"/> When they shall rise - This clause is wanting in BCDL, four others, Syriac, later Arabic, later Persic, Coptic, Saxon, and two of the Itala. Griesbach leaves it doubtful.
entries.5462557ebdae08f81941a79c0dfcb1bf6a356473: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen39584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39585" type="x-p"/> But the God of the living - Θεος, God, is left out by ABCDKL, and in more than forty others, Syriac, one Arabic, one Persic, Coptic, Armenian, Gothic, Saxon, Vulgate, Itala, and Origen. Griesbach has omitted it.
entries.265d3c7609125d169b70f3bb50bdd5324112334c: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen39585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39586" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt love the Lord - On the nature and properties of the love of God and man, and the way in which this commandment is fulfilled, see the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.22.37">Mat 22:37</reference>, etc.
entries.e45c2b4ac16306a3beec5f96b86fa7deab81a87a: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen39586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39587" type="x-p"/> And the scribe said - The answer of the scribe, contained in <reference osisRef="Mar.12.32-Mar.12.34">Mar 12:32-34</reference>, is not found either in Matthew or Luke. This is another proof against Mark's supposed abridgment.
entries.a6262210c9989318a03e9204e3bf8fd3b94086e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen39587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39588" type="x-p"/> Thou art not far from the kingdom of God - This scribe appears to have been a prudent, sensible, and pious man; almost a Christian - so near the kingdom of God that he might have easily stepped in. It is very probable that he did at last believe in and confess Jesus.
entries.53a47e9fd03b7a7befb792aac8fc1f8ef8584536: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen39588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39589" type="x-p"/> How say the scribes - See <reference osisRef="Mat.22.41">Mat 22:41</reference>, etc.
entries.a8aae7d4ebf85c22496784ea8eefbc89cfe0186b: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen39589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39590" type="x-p"/> The common people heard him gladly - And were doubtless many of them brought to believe and receive the truth. By the comparatively poor the Gospel is still best received.
entries.b6451a4ec5f4edf918ec5fdb10041530378e00f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen39590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39591" type="x-p"/> Beware of the scribes - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.23.1">Mat 23:1</reference> (note), etc.
entries.80d441fd64c82d0af46a029d0b736e5299ffc8e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen39591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39592" type="x-p"/> Cast money into the treasury - It is worthy of observation, that the money put into the treasury, even by the rich, is termed by the evangelist χαλκον, brass money, probably that species of small brass coin which was called פרוטה prutah among the Jews, two of which make a farthing, and twenty-four an Italian assarius, which assarius is the twenty-fourth part of a silver penny. We call this, mite, from the French, miete, which signifies a crumb, or very small morsel. The prutah was the smallest coin in use among the Jews: and there is a canon among the rabbins that no person shall put less than two prutahs into the treasury. This poor widow would not give less, and her poverty prevented her from giving more. And whereas it is said that many rich persons cast in Much, πολλα, (many), this may only refer to the number of the prutahs which they threw in, and not to the value. What opinion should we form of a rich man, who, in a collection for a public charity, only threw in a handful of halfpence? See <reference osisRef="Luk.21.1">Luk 21:1</reference>, and see the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.5.26">Mat 5:26</reference>. The whole of this account is lacking in Matthew. Another proof that Mark did not abridge him. <div eID="gen39592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39593" type="x-p"/> Let us examine this subject a little more closely: Jesus prefers the widow's two mites to all the offerings made by the rich. <div eID="gen39593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39594" type="x-p"/> In the preceding account, <reference osisRef="Mar.12.41">Mar 12:41</reference>, it is said Jesus beheld how the people cast money into the treasury. To make this relation the more profitable, let us consider Christ the observer and judge of human actions. <div eID="gen39594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39595" type="x-p"/> I. Christ the observer. <div eID="gen39595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39596" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ observes all men and all things: all our actions are before his eyes, what we do in public and what we do in private are equally known unto him. <div eID="gen39596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39597" type="x-p"/> 2. He observes the state and situation we are in: his eye was upon the abundance of the rich who had given much; and he was well acquainted with the poverty and desolate state of the widow who had given her all, though that was but little in itself. What an awful thought for the rich! "God sees every penny I possess, and constantly observes how I lay it out." What a comfortable thought for the poor and desolate! The eye of the most merciful and bountiful Jesus continually beholds my poverty and distress, and will cause them to work for my good. <div eID="gen39597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39598" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ sees all the motives which lead men to perform their respective actions; and the different motives which lead them to perform the same action: he knows whether they act through vanity, self-love, interest, ambition, hypocrisy, or whether through love, charity, zeal for his glory, and a hearty desire to please him. <div eID="gen39598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39599" type="x-p"/> 4. He observes the circumstances which accompany our actions; whether we act with care or negligence, with a ready mind or with reluctance. <div eID="gen39599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39600" type="x-p"/> 5. He observes the judgment which we form of that which we do in his name; whether we esteem ourselves more on account of what we have done, speak of it to others, dwell on our labors, sufferings, expenses, success, etc., or whether we humble ourselves because we have done so little good, and even that little in so imperfect a way. <div eID="gen39600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39601" type="x-p"/> II. See the judgment Christ forms of our actions. <div eID="gen39601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39602" type="x-p"/> 1. He appears surprised that so much piety should be found with so much poverty, in this poor widow. <div eID="gen39602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39603" type="x-p"/> 2. He shows that works of charity, etc., should be estimated, not by their appearance, but by the spirit which produces them. <div eID="gen39603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39604" type="x-p"/> 3. He shows by this that all men are properly in a state of equality; for though there is and ought to be a difference in outward things, yet God looks upon the heart, and the poorest person has it in his power to make his mite as acceptable to the Lord, by simplicity of intention, and purity of affection, as the millions given by the affluent. It is just in God to rate the value of an action by the spirit in which it is done. <div eID="gen39604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39605" type="x-p"/> 4. He shows that men should judge impartially in cases of this kind, and not permit themselves to be carried away to decide for a person by the largeness of the gift on the one hand, or against him by the smallness of the bounty on the other. Of the poor widow it is said, She has cast in more than all the rich. Because: 1. She gave more; she gave her all, and they gave only a part. 2. She did this in a better spirit, having a simple desire to please God. Never did any king come near the liberality of this widow; she gave all that she had, ὁλον τον βιον αὑτης, her whole life, i.e. all that she had to provide for one day's sustenance, and could have no more till by her labor she had acquired it. What trust must there be in the Divine Providence to perform such an act as this! <div eID="gen39605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39606" type="x-p"/> Two important lessons may be learned from her conduct. 1. A lesson of humiliation to the rich, who, by reason of covetousness on the one hand, and luxury on the other, give but little to God and the poor. A lesson of reproof to the poor, who, through distrust of God's providence, give nothing at all. Our possessions can only be sanctified by giving a portion to God. There will be infallibly a blessing in the remainder, when a part has been given to God and the poor. If the rich and the poor reflect seriously on this, the one will learn pity, the other liberality, and both be blessed in their deed. He must be a poor man indeed who cannot find one poorer than himself.  <chapter eID="Mark.12"/> <div eID="gen39606" type="x-p"/>

entries.1f9a83d2b241498c29c390e2bdfe57bc9feb0039: Verse 37. The common people heard him gladly. The success of our Saviour in his preaching was chiefly among the common or the poorer class of people. entries.4b27051d401c4c9428af416451c686c5ad8935fd:
Verse 44. Of their abundance. Of their superfluous store. They have given what they did not need. They could afford it as well as not; and in doing it they have shown no self-denial.

She of her want. Of her poverty.

All her living. All that she had to live on. She trusted in God to supply her wants, and devoted her little property entirely to him. From this passage we may learn:

(1.) That God is pleased with offerings made to him and his cause.

(2.) That it is our duty to devote our property to God. We received it from him; and we shall not employ it in a proper manner unless we feel that we are stewards, and ask of him what we shall do with it. Jesus approved the conduct of all who had given money to the treasury.

(3.) That the highest evidence of love to the cause of religion is not the amount given, but the amount compared with our means.

(4.) That it may be proper to give all our property to God, and to depend on his Providence for the supply of our wants.

(5.) That God does not despise the humblest offering, if made in sincerity, He loves a cheerful giver.

(6.) That there are none who may not in this way show their love to the cause of religion. There are few, very few scholars in all our Sabbath schools, who may not give as much to the cause of religion as this poor widow; and Jesus would be as ready to approve their offerings as he was hers, and the time to begin to be benevolent and to do good is in early life, in childhood.

(7.) That it is every man's duty to make inquiry, not how much he gives, but how much compared with what he has; how much self-denial he practises, and what is the motive with which it is done.

(8.) We may remark that few practise self-denial for the purposes of charity. Most give of their abundance--that is, what they can spare without feeling it--and many feel that this is the same as throwing it away. Among all the thousands who give to these objects, how few deny themselves of one comfort, even the least, that they may advance the kingdom of Christ!

entries.954f23f30a1c582ba438e969793881bfcc96a846: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.12.32" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.12.32" sID="gen101710" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.12.32">Mark 12:32</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Master, thou hast spoken well, and with truth. Mark </hi>alone mentions that the <hi type="italic">scribe </hi>was softened down; and it is worthy of notice that, though he had attacked Christ maliciously, and with the intention of taking him by surprise, not only does he silently yield to the latter, but openly and candidly assents to what Christ had said. Thus we see that he did not belong to the class of those enemies whose obstinacy is incurable; for, though they have been a hundred times convinced, yet they do not cease to oppose the truth in some manner. From this reply it may also be concluded, that Christ did not precisely include under these two words the rule of life, but embraced the opportunity which presented itself for reproving the false and hypocritical holiness of the scribes, who, giving their whole attention to outward ceremonies, almost entirely disregarded the spiritual worship of God, and cared little about brotherly kindness. Now though the scribe was infected by such corruptions, yet, as sometimes happens, he had obtained from the Law the seed of right knowledge, which lay choked in his heart, and on that account he easily allows himself to be withdrawn from the wicked custom.<div eID="gen101711" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.12.32" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101710" osisID="Mark.12.32" type="section"/>
entries.b218dddb310a6e6f4a30b20916b419c65924f969: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.12.33" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.12.33" sID="gen101712" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101713" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">33.</hi> <hi type="italic">Is better than all burnt-offerings and sacrifices. </hi>But it appears to be incongruous that <hi type="italic">sacrifices, </hi>which are a part of divine worship, and belong to the first table of the Law, should be reckoned of less importance than charity towards men. The reply is, Though the worship of God is greatly preferable, and is more valuable than all the duties of a holy life, yet its outward exercises ought not to be estimated so highly as to swallow up brotherly kindness. For we know that brotherly kindness, in itself and simply, is pleasing to God, though <hi type="italic">sacrifices </hi>are not regarded by him with delight or approbation, except with a view to another object. Besides, it is naked and empty <hi type="italic">sacrifices </hi>that are here spoken of; for our Lord contrasts a hypocritical appearance of piety with true and sincere uprightness. The same doctrine is to be found very frequently in the prophets, that hypocrites may know that <hi type="italic">sacrifices </hi>are of no value, unless spiritual truth be joined to them, and that God is not appeased by offerings of beasts, where brotherly kindness is neglected.<div eID="gen101713" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.12.33" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101712" osisID="Mark.12.33" type="section"/>

34. But when Jesus saw. Whether this scribe made any farther progress is uncertain; but as he had shown himself to be teachable, Christ stretches out the hand to him, and teaches us, by his example, that we ought to assist those in whom there is any beginning either of docility or of right understanding. There appear to have been two reasons why Christ declared that this scribe was not far from the kingdom of God. It was because he was easily persuaded to do his duty, and because he skillfully distinguished the outward worship of God from necessary duties. Nor was it so much with the design of praising as of exhorting him, that Christ declared that he was near the kingdom of God; and in his person Christ encourages us all, after having once entered into the right path, to proceed with so much the greater cheerfulness. By these words we are also taught that many, while they are still held and involved in error, advance with closed eyes towards the road, and in this manner are prepared for running in the course of the Lord, when the time arrives.
And after that, no man ventured to put a question to him. The assertion of the Evangelists, that the mouth of adversaries was stopped, so they did not venture any more to lay snares for Christ, must not be so understood as if’ they desisted from their wicked obstinacy; for they groaned within, like wild beasts shut up in their dens, or, like unruly horses, they bit the bridle. But the more hardened their obstinacy, and the more incorrigible their rebellion, so much the more illustrious was Christ’s triumph over both. And this victory, which he obtained, ought greatly to encourage us never to become dispirited in the defense of the truth, being assured of success. It will often happen, indeed, that enemies shall molest and insult us till the end, but God will at length secure that their fury shall recoil on their own heads, and that, in spite of their efforts, truth shall be victorious.

Mark 12:43. Verily I say to you. This reply of Christ contains a highly useful doctrine that whatever men offer to God ought to be estimated not by its apparent value,
“Selon le prix qu’il vaut au monde;” — “according to the price at which it is estimated by the world.”
but only by the feeling of the heart, and that the holy affection of him who according to his small means, offers to God the little that he has, is more worthy of esteem than that of him who offers a hundred times more out of his abundance. In two ways this doctrine is useful, for the poor who appear not to have the power of doing good, are encouraged by our Lord not to hesitate to express their affection cheerfully out of their slender means; for if they consecrate themselves, their offering, which appears to be mean and worthless, will not be less valuable than if they had presented all the treasures of Crœsus.
“De Crœsus, lequel on dit avoir esté si riche;” — “of Crœsus, who is said to have been so rich.” — The allusion is to Crœsus, King of Lydia, whose vast wealth was a proverb among the Greeks and Romans. — Ed.
On the other hand, those who possess greater abundance, and who have received from God larger communications, are reminded that it is not enough if in the amount of their beneficence they greatly surpass the poor and common people; because it is of less value in the sight of God that a rich man, out of a vast heap, should bestow a moderate sum, than that a poor man, by giving very little, should exhaust his store. This widow must have been a person of no ordinary piety, who, rather than come empty into the presence of God, chose to part with her own living. And our Lord applauds this sincerity, because, forgetting herself, she wished to testify that she and all that she possessed belonged to God. In like manner, the chief sacrifice which God requires from us is self-denial. As to the sacred offerings, it is probable that they were not at that time applied properly, or to lawful purposes; but as the service of the Law was still in force, Christ does not reject them. And certainly the abuses of men could not prevent the sincere worshippers of God from doing what was holy, and in accordance with the command of God, when they offered for sacrifices and other pious uses.

They denyed the <ns0:hi>Immortality of the Soul,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Resurrection of the Body,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Angels,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Spirits, Acts</ns0:hi> 23.8. attributed all to <ns0:hi>free Will,</ns0:hi> denying <ns0:hi>Fate</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stiny,</ns0:hi> they rejected <ns0:hi>Traditions,</ns0:hi> and owned no <ns0:hi>Scriptures,</ns0:hi> but the Five Books of <ns0:hi>Moses.</ns0:hi> They seemed to be a kind of <ns0:hi>Ratio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nal Divines,</ns0:hi> that would own, and believe nothing, but what they could Fathom by their Reason, or was Obvious to their Sense; and their Doctrine was excellently Suited to Mens Lusts, who desire not to be troubled with any thoughts of a World to come. Nothing more shews the Degeneracy, and Debauchery of humane Nature than this; That to Gratify their Sensual Ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />petites, more feely in the things of this Life, they will be content to think of <ns0:hi>Annihilation</ns0:hi> (which Nature not Debauched abhors) and of quitting all Hopes of Eternal Life and Happiness, that they may have a Principle to warrant their living like Beasts; they come to our Saviour, thinking to flout him and his Hearers out of the Doctrine of the <ns0:hi>Resurrection,</ns0:hi> as having insuperable diffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culties to Clog it. But he that takes the wise in their own Craf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiness, shews these wise Men, that all their Wisdom was but Fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, and their Argument wholly proceeded <ns0:hi>ex ignoratione Elen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chi,</ns0:hi> from their not understanding the thing they would <ns0:hi>Philoso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phise</ns0:hi> about.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="26">26 And as touching the dead, that they rise, have ye not read in the book of Moses, how in the bush God spake unto him, saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 3.6.</ns0:note> I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> the God of Abra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 He is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living, ye therefore do greatly err.<ns0:note place="bottom">The true question about the <ns0:hi>Resurrection,</ns0:hi> was, Whether <ns0:hi>the Bodies of the Dead shall rise or no</ns0:hi>? not whether they shall a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rise with the same <ns0:hi>Qualities, Affections, Powers,</ns0:hi> &c. they are sown <ns0:hi>Natural,</ns0:hi> but they shall arise <ns0:hi>Spiritual Bodies,</ns0:hi> without Af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fections and Qualities disposing them to Actions, only necessary for the supporting the <ns0:hi>Natural Life.</ns0:hi> Such as <ns0:hi>Hunger</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Thirst,</ns0:hi> &c. or for the upholding the World, that while one Generation passeth, it might be supplyed by another. Such as an Appetite to Marriage, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> What needs this when all Generations shall be de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />termined in the everlasting World? So as in Truth these Learned Men, shewed themselves Dunces, wholly ignorant of what they came to argue upon. They should first have proved that there would be any need of Wives, or any such thing as Marriage, af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter the World should have an end. In the mean time our Saviour proveth the Resurrection out of the Writings of Moses, owned by themselves for Holy Writ. Without a Resurrection <ns0:hi>Abra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ham</ns0:hi> would not be <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> nor <ns0:hi>Isaac Isaac,</ns0:hi> nor <ns0:hi>Iacob Ia<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cob,</ns0:hi> see the Notes on this part of the History, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 22.24, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>

For the understanding of this History, both as to the Letter, and profitable Instruction arising from it we must know, That in the <ns0:hi>Temple</ns0:hi> (where our Saviour now was) there was a <ns0:hi>Treasury,</ns0:hi> or rather <ns0:hi>Treasuries.</ns0:hi> And famous Dr. <ns0:hi>Lightfoot</ns0:hi> saith, there were <ns0:hi>Treasure Chambers</ns0:hi> called <ns0:hi>Lesacoth,</ns0:hi> and thirteen <ns0:hi>Trea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure-Chests</ns0:hi> called <ns0:hi>Shopheroth,</ns0:hi> all called by the General Name of <ns0:hi>Corban</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Corbonah.</ns0:hi> Two of these Chests were for the <ns0:hi>half-shekel,</ns0:hi> which every <ns0:hi>Israelite</ns0:hi> was to pay according to the Law, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 30.12, 13.
